claims.claim: Existentialism is a loose family of ideas, not a tidy school.
claims.evidence: SEP intro: 'certainly not a reference to a coherent system or philosophical school' ... 'a set of overlapping ideas that bind the movement together'

claims.claim: It starts from life as a person lives it, not from a detached viewpoint.
claims.evidence: SEP 2: 'we cannot look down on the human condition from a detached, third-person perspective' ... 'begins from the standpoint of the engagé'

claims.claim: Its central idea is that we are not born with a fixed nature.
claims.evidence: SEP intro lists five 'overlapping ideas' (Nihilism, Engagement, Existence Precedes Essence, Freedom, Authenticity, Ethics) and says 'there is no unifying doctrine'. No cited section ranks existence-precedes-essence as THE central idea; calling it central contradicts the 'no unifying doctrine' line the same paragraph relies on.

claims.claim: We make ourselves through our choices.
claims.evidence: SEP intro: 'burdened with the task of creating ourselves through our choices and actions'

claims.claim: We are responsible for who we become.
claims.evidence: SEP intro: 'we are free and responsible for who we are and what we do'

claims.claim: Two nineteenth-century thinkers laid the groundwork: Kierkegaard and Nietzsche.
claims.evidence: SEP intro: 'the conceptual groundwork of the movement was laid much earlier in the nineteenth century by pioneers like Søren Kierkegaard and Friedrich Nietzsche'. Note: 'pioneers like' gives examples; 'Two' reads as exhaustive, acceptable since source names no other 19th-century pioneer.

claims.claim: Kierkegaard was from Denmark.
claims.evidence: SEP Kierkegaard 1: 'born ... in Copenhagen ... He spent most of his life in and around the Danish capital'

claims.claim: Nietzsche was a German philosopher.
claims.evidence: SEP Nietzsche intro: 'was a German philosopher and cultural critic'

claims.claim: In mid-twentieth-century France, Sartre and Beauvoir made it famous.
claims.evidence: SEP intro: 'exploded on the scene in mid-twentieth-century France' ... 'the most popular voices of this movement were French, most notably Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir'

items.fix: Replace 'Its central idea is that' with 'One of its core ideas is that' (SEP intro: overlapping ideas, no unifying doctrine).

claims.claim: It rejects fixed moral rules.
claims.evidence: SEP intro: 'they reject the idea of moral absolutes and universalizing judgments about right conduct'

claims.claim: It does not say that morality is empty.
claims.evidence: SEP intro: 'existentialism should not be dismissed for promoting moral nihilism'

claims.claim: A good life is possible: one where we own our choices and help others be free too.
claims.evidence: SEP intro: 'a moral or praiseworthy life is possible. It is one where we acknowledge and own up to our freedom, take full responsibility for our choices, and act in such a way as to help others realize their freedom.'

claims.claim: Above all, it takes on questions we all meet.
claims.evidence: Cited SEP intro gives no ranking; it names 'the anxiety-provoking givens of death, freedom, and meaninglessness' that a generation 'was forced to confront', but nothing says these questions come 'above all' (e.g. above its ethics, just stated). Minor sharpening.

claims.claim: Question: How do I live when no rulebook tells me how?
claims.evidence: SEP intro: 'reject the idea of moral absolutes and universalizing judgments about right conduct'

claims.claim: Question: How do I stop drifting along with the crowd?
claims.evidence: SEP intro: 'critical of our ingrained tendency to conform to the norms and expectations of the public world'

claims.claim: Question: How do I face anxiety, death and a sense that life is meaningless?
claims.evidence: SEP intro: 'confront the human condition and the anxiety-provoking givens of death, freedom, and meaninglessness'

items.fix: Drop 'Above all,': 'It also takes on questions we all meet:'.

claims.claim: We are not born with a fixed nature.
claims.evidence: SEP 3 (theme source): 'there is no pre-given or essential nature that determines us'; SEP intro: 'not as a substance or thing with some pre-given nature'

claims.claim: We make ourselves through what we choose.
claims.evidence: SEP 3: 'we are always in the process of making or defining ourselves through the situated choices we make'

claims.claim: Sartre called 'existence precedes essence' the first principle of existentialism.
claims.evidence: SEP 3: 'Sartre will later repackage this line with the pithy adage, “existence precedes essence” ... This is, according to Sartre, “the first principle of existentialism,”'

claims.claim: Gloss: 'essence' would be a fixed nature that decides who you are.
claims.evidence: SEP intro: 'some pre-given nature (or “essence”)'; SEP 3: 'pre-given or essential nature that determines us'

claims.claim: Existentialists say there is no such essence.
claims.evidence: SEP 3: 'there is no pre-given or essential nature that determines us'

claims.claim: A person first 'turns up' and only afterwards defines himself.
claims.evidence: SEP 3: 'man exists, turns up, appears on the scene, and, only afterwards, defines himself'

claims.claim: ...through choices made as life unfolds.
claims.evidence: SEP 3: 'through the situated choices we make as our lives unfold'

claims.claim: Sartre adapted the idea from Heidegger.
claims.evidence: SEP 3: 'initially introduced early on in Heidegger’s Being and Time ... Sartre will later repackage this line'

claims.claim: Heidegger was a German philosopher.
claims.evidence: SEP intro: 'twentieth-century German philosophers like Edmund Husserl, Martin Heidegger, and Karl Jaspers'

claims.claim: Hard facts still limit us, such as our body and the time and place we live in.
claims.evidence: SEP 3: 'determinate aspects or “facts” about our situation that limit and constrain us ... our embodiment and spatiality ... and the socio-historical context we find ourselves in'

claims.claim: Gloss: existentialists call these facts our 'facticity'.
claims.evidence: SEP 3: 'This is our givenness (or “facticity”)'

claims.claim: We can question them, give them meaning and decide what to do with them.
claims.evidence: SEP 3: 'surpass our facticity by calling it into question, interpreting it in different ways, and making decisions about how to deal with it in the future'

claims.claim: Gloss: this power to rise above the facts is called 'transcendence'.
claims.evidence: SEP 3: 'we have the capacity to rise above or “transcend” these facts' ... 'tension between “facticity” and “transcendence”'

claims.claim: If nothing fixed decides who we are, then we are free.
claims.evidence: SEP 4: 'Recognizing that there is no pre-given essence that determines existence ... it is up to the individual to make ... their own identity'

claims.claim: We are also responsible for what we make of ourselves.
claims.evidence: SEP 4: 'can be held responsible for their actions' ... 'we alone are responsible for our choices and the projects we undertake'

claims.claim: Sartre's coward: childhood or genes did not make him that way; he 'makes himself a coward' by his decisions.
claims.evidence: SEP 4: 'the coward ... is not the way he is because of an unstable childhood or a particular genetic makeup. The coward “makes himself a coward” by means of his decisions'

claims.claim: Seeing this brings anxiety.
claims.evidence: SEP 4: 'the awareness is often accompanied by anxiety because we realize that we alone are responsible'

claims.claim: No god and no absolute moral rule can choose for us or excuse us.
claims.evidence: SEP 4: 'There is no moral absolute, divine will, or natural law that can provide guidance or justify our actions.'

claims.claim: Sartre: 'no excuses behind us nor justifications before us'.
claims.evidence: SEP 4: '“there are no excuses behind us nor justifications before us” (Sartre 1946 [2001, 296])' - verbatim

claims.claim: Kierkegaard called anxiety 'the dizziness of freedom'.
claims.evidence: SEP Kierkegaard 2: 'Haufniensis, who says that anxiety is the dizziness of freedom'. Note: the source attributes it to his pseudonym Vigilius Haufniensis; acceptable for beginners, meaning unchanged.

claims.claim: Existentialists ask us to face this feeling, not run from it.
claims.evidence: SEP 5.1: 'Instead of turning away from this basic anxiety, the existentialist asks us to turn toward and face it'

claims.claim: It can shake us out of our comfortable routines.
claims.evidence: SEP 5.1: 'uncanny affects that have the power to shake us out of our complacency'

claims.claim: Most of the time we just do what everyone else does.
claims.evidence: SEP 5: 'we tend to get pulled along by the crowd, doing what “they” do'

claims.claim: Being authentic means living our own life.
claims.evidence: SEP 5: 'Rather than living our own lives, we tend to get pulled along by the crowd'; SEP intro: 'authentic or true to ourselves'

claims.claim: Gloss: being authentic means being true to yourself.
claims.evidence: SEP intro: 'prevents us from being authentic or true to ourselves' - quote verbatim

claims.claim: Existentialists criticise living by rules and expectations we pick up from others.
claims.evidence: SEP intro: 'critical of our ingrained tendency to conform to the norms and expectations of the public world'

claims.claim: Heidegger: we enjoy, read and judge things as 'they' do.
claims.evidence: SEP 5: '“We take pleasure and enjoy ourselves as they take pleasure. We read, see, and judge about literature and art as they see and judge”'

claims.claim: Doing what everyone does is comforting, because it feels like living well.
claims.evidence: SEP 5: 'Living this way can be comforting, creating the illusion that we are living well because we are doing what everyone else does.'

claims.claim: But it hides our freedom from us.
claims.evidence: SEP 5: 'we are unwilling or unable to face up to the freedom and contingency of our condition'; '“tranquilizing” ... because it covers over the anxiety of own freedom and finitude'

claims.claim: Sartre and Beauvoir call this self-deception 'bad faith'.
claims.evidence: SEP 5: 'Sartre and Beauvoir refer to inauthenticity in terms of “bad faith” (mauvaise foi)'

claims.claim: I am in bad faith when I treat myself as a fixed thing: 'I am what I am'.
claims.evidence: SEP 5.5: 'the most common ... form of bad faith is when I over-identify with my facticity, as if I were a fully realized object or thing ... that “I am what I am”'

claims.claim: I am also in bad faith when I pretend my situation puts no limits on my choices.
claims.evidence: SEP 5: 'I am also in bad faith when I over-identify with freedom and deny ... the fact that my choices are limited and constrained by my situation.'

claims.claim: Kierkegaard's name for the crowd: 'the public'.
claims.evidence: SEP 1: 'In their conceptions of “the public” (Kierkegaard), “the herd” (Nietzsche), and “the They” (Heidegger)'

claims.claim: Nietzsche's name for the crowd: 'the herd'.
claims.evidence: SEP 1: same line

claims.claim: Heidegger's name for the crowd: 'the They'.
claims.evidence: SEP 1: same line

claims.claim: What authenticity looks like varies by thinker.
claims.evidence: SEP 5.2-5.5 give separate accounts per thinker

claims.claim: Kierkegaard: a passionate commitment that pulls a scattered life together.
claims.evidence: SEP 5.2: 'a passionate, “personality defining” ... decision or commitment that binds together and unifies the fragmented and disjointed moments of our life into a focused and coherent whole'

claims.claim: Nietzsche: saying yes to your whole life, even to living it again forever.
claims.evidence: SEP 5.3: 'The Overman is a “yes-sayer” who affirms every aspect of his life' ... eternal recurrence: 'live the same life we are living now over and over for eternity'

claims.evidence: SEP 5.4: '“resoluteness” ... “pull [myself] together,” giving life a sense of cohesion and focus ... I must also be willing to let go or give up on them depending on the circumstances'

claims.claim: Sartre and Beauvoir: seeing your unsettled situation clearly, accepting it, and taking responsibility for what you do.
claims.evidence: SEP 5.5: 'a clear-eyed awareness and acceptance of the instability and ambiguity of the human condition ... a willingness to act ... and to take responsibility'

claims.claim: Albert Camus was a French novelist.

claims.claim: Camus called our situation 'the absurd'.

claims.claim: Beauvoir held that existence is not absurd but ambiguous: its meaning is never fixed, so we keep making it.

Note: placed right after Camus, a reader may take it as a rebuttal of Camus; the source does not link the two, and Beauvoir's 'absurd' (no meaning can ever be given) is not Camus's (a clash). Not counted as drift.

claims.claim: Gloss: a 'knight of faith' is someone who commits to a truth that reason cannot make sense of.
claims.evidence: SEP 5.2: 'he is confronted with a personal truth that is higher than the universal. In committing himself to this truth, Abraham becomes a “knight of faith” by “leaping” into a paradox, one where the truth of “the singular individual is higher than the universal”'. The gloss keeps the irrationality but drops the defining point: a personal truth that overrides the universal moral duty (to protect his son). For a beginner it now reads as 'believing something irrational', not 'putting a personal truth above morality'.

claims.claim: His 'underground man' refuses to be reduced to 'a piano key' in a world run by fixed laws.
claims.evidence: SEP 4.1: 'rebels against an increasingly scientized, rational, and mechanistic picture of human behavior promoted by Russian social reformers in the 1860s, where everything a person does was thought to be determined by causal laws. For the underground man, this view reduces the human being to ... “a piano key”'. The source says he rebels against a VIEW that causal laws determine human behaviour; the text states as fact that the world is run by fixed laws, which flips the point (his revolt affirms that we are not so determined). Quote 'a piano key' is verbatim.

items.fix: '...whose "underground man" refuses to be reduced to "a piano key" by a view that causal laws decide everything a person does.'
